Class Pico2WTrustZoneStore

java.lang.Object
io.github.jabrena.juno.hardware.security.Pico2WTrustZoneStore
All Implemented Interfaces:
SecretStore
public final class Pico2WTrustZoneStore extends Object
Named-secret storage on the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W, kept by Juno's own TrustZone secure firmware: the RP2350 has no secure element, so a small program in the Cortex-M33's secure world holds the slots in a flash sector it fences off, and this program, which runs in the non-secure world, reaches them only through that firmware's one gateway. Each slot holds one name with its value.

juno:flash installs the firmware with any program that uses this store: it takes the 12 KB boot slot arduino-pico normally gives its OTA stage, so nothing else has to be flashed first. A program flashed without it, for example one that does not use the store, runs as usual but replaces the firmware; the slots are still in their sector, unfenced, until a program that uses the store is flashed again.

Stronger than Esp32Nvs, weaker than a secure element. The fence is enforced by the CPU: code in this program, its libraries included, can read a secret only through SecretStore.read(String, byte[]), and a direct read of the sector faults. The board is never locked, though: no fuse is written and debug stays on, so anyone holding the board and a USB cable can still read or replace the whole flash. The values are not encrypted.

Programs that use it run on one carrier: the second core cannot be started from the non-secure world, so virtual threads on two carriers are rejected when the program is compiled.

Callers should obtain it through MCU.getSecretStore(), which keeps the store choice out of application code.

    • isAvailable

    • read

      public int read(String key, byte[] buffer)
      Description copied from interface: SecretStore
      Copies the value of key into buffer and returns its length, or a negative value when the name is not stored, the store does not answer, or the value is longer than buffer. Allocates nothing; buffer is written only on success.
      Specified by:
      read in interface SecretStore

    • write

      public int write(String key, byte[] value, int length)
      Description copied from interface: SecretStore
      Stores value[0..length) under key, replacing whatever that name held, and returns length. A new name takes a free slot. A length of 0 clears the name. Returns a negative value when the name is not valid, the bytes do not fit next to the name, every slot already holds another name, or the store refuses the write. A failed write may leave the name partly rewritten, so the caller should write it again. Writes come from provisioning code, not from programs that only read secrets.
      Specified by:
      write in interface SecretStore

    • clear

      public int clear(String key)
      Description copied from interface: SecretStore
      Empties key, so that a later SecretStore.read(String, byte[]) reports it missing. Returns 0 on success, including when the name was not stored, or -1 when the name is not valid or the store refuses the write.
      Specified by:
      clear in interface SecretStore

    • clearAll

      public int clearAll()
      Description copied from interface: SecretStore
      Empties every slot of the store, whichever program wrote it: it decommissions the store, so a secret another program provisioned is erased too. Use SecretStore.clear(String) in a loop over the names a program owns to empty just those. Tries every slot even after a failure, and returns 0 when all were cleared or -1 when any slot refused the write.
      Specified by:
      clearAll in interface SecretStore

    • getString

      public @Nullable String getString(String key)
      Description copied from interface: SecretStore
      Returns the value of key as a String, or null when it is missing. Allocates one String, so call it once at startup.
